back: Applying knowledge, skills, tools and techniques to determine problems and opportunities, recommend solutions, elicit and manage requirements, and define and measure value.
Anyone who performs business analysis, whatever the job title.

front: Business analyst vs project manager: responsible for
back: Business analyst: the product. Project manager: the project.
Product scope: the features and functions of the solution. Project scope: the work performed to deliver it.
A condition or capability that must be present in a product, service or result to satisfy a business need.

front: The four types of product requirement
back: Business, stakeholder, solution (functional and nonfunctional) and transition.
The higher-level need of the organization: why the work is being done. Usually defined before the project starts.
The needs of a stakeholder or stakeholder group.
The features, functions and characteristics of a product that will meet the business and stakeholder requirements.
Describes the behaviors of the product: what it does.
Describes the conditions or qualities needed for the product to be effective: reliability, security, performance, safety.
A temporary capability, such as data conversion or training, needed to move from the current state to the future state.
An action, process or condition the project must meet, such as a milestone date. Part of project management, not business analysis.
A condition or criterion used to validate that a project deliverable is complete, such as a test or certification. Part of project management.
An artifact that is produced and quantifiable. Tangible or intangible: a device, a process, a service.
Something produced to deliver measurable business value and meet the business need: a new product, part of a product, or an enhancement.
The phases of a product from concept through delivery, growth, maturity and maintenance to retirement. May contain several project life cycles.

front: Where does business analysis sit in the life cycles?
back: Across the whole product life cycle: before a project (needs assessment), during it (requirements) and after it (evaluation).
Everything business analysis creates and uses about the product: goals, requirements, models, backlogs, user stories, acceptance criteria, risks, assumptions, constraints, issues.
The net quantifiable benefit derived from a business endeavor. Tangible, intangible or both.

front: When should the measure of business value be decided?
back: Before the project starts, with a baseline taken, because benefits often appear well after the project ends.

front: The six business analysis process groups
back: Defining and Aligning, Initiating, Planning, Executing, Monitoring and Controlling, Releasing.
Investigates whether a new or changed product is viable and aligns products and projects with strategy. Happens before and after projects.
Decides whether all or part of a solution should be released, and obtains acceptance that it is ready to hand over.

front: The six business analysis knowledge areas
back: Needs Assessment, Stakeholder Engagement, Elicitation, Analysis, Traceability and Monitoring, Solution Evaluation.

front: How many business analysis processes are there?
back: 35, across 6 knowledge areas and 6 process groups.

front: Which knowledge area interacts with all the others?
back: Stakeholder Engagement.

front: Which three knowledge areas tend to be used at the same time?
back: Elicitation, Analysis, and Traceability and Monitoring.
Choosing the processes, techniques, level of detail and deliverables that fit a particular effort.
An individual with decision-making authority for prioritizing what to include in or exclude from a product.
An individual responsible for achieving customer and market success for a product.
The person responsible for a business process that the solution must fit into or will change.
Everyone on the project team is on the product team, but the product team also includes people not assigned to the project.

front: How does a business analyst lead?
back: By influence, without supervisory authority: through trust, honesty, integrity and transparency. A trusted advisor.

front: Business analysis on an agile team
back: The work is still done but is often spread across the team. The analyst often helps the product owner refine the backlog.

front: Six categories of business analyst skills
back: Analytical skills, expert judgment, communication skills, personal skills, leadership skills, tool knowledge.

front: What happens when a stakeholder is overlooked?
back: Requirements are likely to be missed.

front: Practices of the Business Value Assessment domain
back: Understand the Situation; Find the Gaps; Define the Solution.

front: Practices of the Solution Refinement domain
back: Elicit Solution Information; Analyze Solution Information; Package Solution Information.

front: Practices of the Business Analysis Stewardship domain
back: Promote Business Analysis Effectiveness; Enhance Business Analysis Capability; Lead Business Analysis Work with Integrity.

front: Practices of Organizational Transition and Solution Evaluation
back: Enable Organizational Transition; Facilitate Go/No-Go Decision; Evaluate Solution Performance.

front: The analyst beside the product owner (adaptive)
back: The analyst can support the product owner, act as proxy, or fill the role. Elaborating backlog items remains the product owner's responsibility.
